description: We're Software Engineering students from UnB competing in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We're building a game where players manage a lunar or Martian base, balancing life support, radiation, energy, and food — our first time making a game, and we're excited. Team's full for this edition, but happy to connect with anyone into game design, 2D/3D art, or sound.
summary:
Dust & Dome is a browser-based 2.5D isometric mission trainer for kids aged 7–12
where players lead four astronauts in Hellas Planitia, Mars, across four Martian years to prepare a self-sustaining colony for 32 new arrivals. Every choice is a real trade-off
between power, life support and protection: build solar panels or a greenhouse, open a new module or save energy for the night, take shelter from a solar storm or keep
working. Martian seasons, dust storms and radiation events, driven by real NASA data,
keep the crew on their toes, and a quick repair challenge lets players fix the base with
their own hands. By the end, kids have learned, by doing, why living on Mars is hard,
and why careful planning is what lets people thrive there.
details:
Dust & Dome is a browser game for kids aged 7–12. Four astronauts land at Hellas Planitia on Mars, where NASA radar found buried water ice. They have four Martian years to build a base that can hold a full season of oxygen, water and food for 32 arriving colonists.

The player builds on an isometric grid, switches machines Off, Min or Max, and decides who works outside. Every choice trades power, life support and protection. Real hazards hit the base: dust devils, dust storms, a freezing winter and radiation storms. Commander Vega briefs the player each season, and every structure has a short science card. When the base fails, a debrief explains the real science behind the cause.

Real science, honestly labeled: radiation storms are modeled on real NASA DONKI solar events, using an archived snapshot (never presented as live). The oxygen generator is based on NASA's MOXIE, and the reactor on NASA's Fission Surface Power project. Every simplification is marked in the game.

Impact: kids learn why Mars is hard by living the trade-offs. It runs from a link, with no download or login, in English and Portuguese, on desktop and phone.

Tools: TypeScript, React, three.js (React Three Fiber), Zustand, Zod, Vite and Vitest. We worked spec-first and test-first with GitHub Spec Kit, and used AI assistants, all listed in our credits.

Creative: the Martian year is the game clock, and climate is the antagonist. The game's balance lives in JSON files, so our non-programmer product owners could tune it. We also designed for kids: plain words, large touch targets, and colour never the only signal.
